subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalamu alaikum, young scientist! Look around you right now. The wooden stool you might be sitting on is a solid. The water in the cup beside you is a liquid. The air you are breathing in and out is a gas. Without even thinking about it, you are surrounded by all three states of matter at every single moment of your day. In this unit you will learn to see the world with new eyes, understanding why ice is hard, why water flows, and why steam rises from a pot of bariis cooking over the fire.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Know that evaporation occurs when a liquid turns into a gas
Know that condensation occurs when a gas turns into a liquid and that it is the reverse of evaporation
Know that air contains water vapour and when this meets a cold surface it may condense
Know that the boiling point of water is 100 °C and the melting point of ice is 0 °C

outcomes: Name and describe the three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas, and give examples of each from your own home.
Explain the particle model — that all matter is made of tiny particles, and describe how those particles are arranged and how they move in each state.
Describe state changes — melting, freezing, evaporation, condensing, and boiling — and explain how heating and cooling cause them.
Explain evaporation and identify the four main factors that make a liquid evaporate faster: temperature, surface area, air movement, and humidity.
Describe the water cycle and explain how evaporation and condensation move water between the ocean, the sky, and the land.
Plan a fair test to investigate what affects evaporation, and record your results carefully.
Use scientific words correctly when you write and talk about matter.
Name two other factors mentioned in the passage that help the fish dry faster.

concepts.title: The Three States of Matter
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with what you can see and touch. Take a look at three things you know well: an ice cube, a cup of water, and the air in the room. These are the three states of the very same substance — water — and yet they behave completely differently. Understanding why is the key that unlocks this whole unit.

A solid keeps its own shape. If you place a stone in a bowl, it stays stone-shaped. If you move it to a bucket, it is still the same shape and the same size. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, which means it does not spread out or squash down easily. Think of the things around your home that are solids: a metal spoon, a wooden stool, a dried date, a bar of soap, a goat's horn. You can pick them up, and they hold their form. When you press a solid, it does not get smaller — solids are very hard to squeeze, or compress.

A liquid is different. It still takes up a fixed amount of space — it has a definite volume — but it does not have a shape of its own. Instead, a liquid takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. Pour water into a tall thin glass and it becomes tall and thin. Pour that same water into a wide flat dish and it spreads out wide and flat. But the amount of water does not change — one cup of water is still one cup of water. Liquids can flow and be poured, which is why you can pour camel milk from a jug into a cup. Like solids, liquids are hard to compress.

A gas is the freest of all. A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume. It spreads out to completely fill whatever container it is in, no matter how big. Blow up a balloon and the air fills every part of it. Let the air out and it spreads across the whole room. You often cannot see gases, but they are truly there. When you feel the warm coastal wind on your face, you are feeling moving air, which is a mixture of gases. When steam rises from a pot, that is water in its gas form. Unlike solids and liquids, gases can be squeezed into a smaller space quite easily, because there is a lot of empty space inside a gas.

The wonderful thing is that the same substance can be all three. Water is a solid when it is frozen as ice, a liquid when you drink it, and a gas when it becomes water vapour. It is still water the whole time — only its state has changed. This idea, that one substance can take three different forms, is at the very heart of this unit.

Let us build a habit right now. At your next meal, look at your plate and cup and try to spot all three states. The bariis (rice) and the goat meat are solids. The water or the camel milk is a liquid. The warm air rising above the hot food, carrying its lovely smell to your nose, is a gas mixed with water vapour. When you can point to solids, liquids, and gases without even thinking, you are already beginning to see the world the way a scientist does.
concepts.example: Did You Know? The air around you is not empty — it is a gas, and it has weight! The air in an ordinary classroom weighs about as much as a small child. Even though you cannot see most gases, you breathe in about 20,000 breaths of them every single day.

concepts.title: The Particle Model - The Secret Inside Matter
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the biggest ideas in all of science. Why does a solid keep its shape while a gas floats away? To answer that, scientists imagine that all matter is built from unbelievably tiny pieces called particles. These particles are far too small to see, even with a normal magnifying glass. A single drop of water contains billions upon billions of them. The way these particles are arranged, and how they move, explains everything about the three states.

In a solid, the particles are packed very closely together in a neat, regular pattern, like dates stacked tightly in a box or bricks in a wall. Strong forces of attraction hold them firmly in place. The particles are not completely still — they vibrate, or jiggle, on the spot — but they cannot move away from their neighbours. Because the particles are locked in position, a solid keeps its shape and its volume. Because they are already so close together, you cannot squeeze a solid any smaller.

In a liquid, the particles are still close together, but they are no longer locked in a fixed pattern. They can slide and roll past one another, a bit like a bag of small dried beans that shift around when you tip the bag. This is why a liquid can flow and take the shape of its container — the particles move to fill the bottom of whatever holds them. But because they are still close together, a liquid keeps a definite volume and is hard to compress.

In a gas, the particles are spread far, far apart with lots of empty space between them. They move quickly in every direction, bouncing off each other and off the walls of their container. There is almost no force holding them together, so they spread out endlessly to fill any space. This is why a gas has no shape and no fixed volume. And because there is so much empty space between the particles, you can squeeze a gas into a much smaller space — the particles simply move closer together.

Here is a helpful picture. Imagine a class of children. When they line up in neat rows, standing still and shoulder to shoulder, that is like a solid. When the same children mill about the classroom, close together but moving around each other, that is like a liquid. When they run freely all over a wide open field, far apart and moving fast in all directions, that is like a gas. The children are the same children — only their arrangement and movement have changed. That is exactly what happens to particles when matter changes state.

[*] Remember! Solid particles: packed tight, vibrate in place, keep their shape. Liquid particles: close together, slide past each other, take the container's shape. Gas particles: far apart, move fast in all directions, fill all the space. The particles themselves do not change — only how they are arranged and how they move.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Particles are always moving, even inside a hard stone. In a solid they only vibrate, but they never fully stop. If you could line up the water particles in a single teaspoon of water in a row, that row would stretch further than you could ever walk.

concepts.title: Changing State - The Power of Heating and Cooling
concepts.explanation:
How does one state turn into another? The answer is energy, and usually that energy comes as heat. When you heat matter, you give its particles more energy, so they move faster and push further apart. When you cool matter, you take energy away, so the particles slow down and move closer together. By adding or removing heat, we can make matter change from solid to liquid to gas, and back again.

When you heat a solid, its particles vibrate faster and faster. At a certain temperature, called the melting point, they gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and begin sliding around each other. The solid has become a liquid. This is melting. You see it when an ice cube melts into water in a warm room, or when a piece of ghee (subag) melts in a hot pan. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius.

Freezing is the opposite of melting. When you cool a liquid, its particles slow down. At the freezing point, they slow so much that the forces of attraction lock them back into fixed positions, and the liquid becomes a solid. Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius — the very same temperature at which ice melts. Notice that melting and freezing are simply the same doorway travelled in opposite directions.

When you heat a liquid, some of its particles gain enough energy to escape from the surface and fly off into the air as a gas. This is evaporation, and we will study it closely in the next section. If you heat the liquid strongly enough, it reaches its boiling point and changes to gas very fast, with bubbles forming all through it — this is boiling. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. When your family boils water on the charcoal jiko to make it safe to drink, you can watch the bubbles rise and the steam pour out.

Condensation is the reverse of evaporation. When water vapour in the air is cooled, its particles slow down and join together to form liquid water again. You have seen this many times: droplets of water forming on the outside of a cold glass of juice, or a misty film on a cool window in the early morning. The water did not leak through the glass — it condensed out of the air.

All of these changes are physical changes, not chemical ones. That means no new substance is made — water is still water whether it is ice, liquid, or vapour. And every one of these changes can be reversed. Melt an ice cube and you can freeze the water again. Boil water into steam and you can cool the steam back into water. This is why the water on Earth has been recycled over and over for millions of years.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Some solids skip the liquid stage completely and turn straight into a gas. This is called sublimation. Dry ice does this, which is how it makes spooky fog. The water you drank today may once have been rain that fell on the Rift Valley, or vapour that rose from the Indian Ocean thousands of years ago.

concepts.title: Evaporation and the Factors That Affect It
concepts.explanation:
Evaporation deserves special attention because it happens all around you, all the time, and understanding it is genuinely useful. Here is the key idea: evaporation can happen at any temperature, not just at boiling point. A puddle in Garissa dries up on a warm morning long before the water is anywhere near boiling. This is because, even in cool water, a few of the fastest-moving particles at the surface always have enough energy to escape into the air. Slowly, one by one, they leave, and the puddle shrinks until it is gone.

Why does wet washing dry faster on some days than others? Why does seawater left in a shallow pan turn to salt more quickly in the sun? The answer is that four main factors control how fast a liquid evaporates. Let us look at each one.

The hotter the liquid or the air around it, the faster it evaporates. Heat gives the particles more energy, so more of them can escape from the surface. This is why Halima hangs the clothes out in the strong afternoon sun rather than in the cool shade — the warmth speeds up evaporation and the clothes dry much faster.

The larger the surface of the liquid that is exposed to the air, the faster it evaporates, because more particles are near the surface where they can escape. A puddle spread out wide and thin dries much faster than the same amount of water in a deep narrow cup. This is exactly why families collecting salt from seawater use wide, shallow pans — the huge surface lets the water evaporate quickly and leaves the salt behind. It is also why we spread washing out flat on the line instead of leaving it bunched in a ball.

Moving air makes evaporation faster. When particles escape from a liquid, they gather in the air just above it. If that damp air sits still, it becomes crowded and some particles fall back into the liquid. But a breeze carries the damp air away and brings fresh dry air, making room for more particles to escape. This is why clothes dry so quickly on a breezy day near the coast, and why waving a wet hand in the wind makes it feel cold as the water evaporates fast.

Humidity is the amount of water vapour already in the air. When the air is dry, it has plenty of room for more water vapour, so evaporation is fast. When the air is very humid — already full of water vapour, as it often is along the damp Indian Ocean coast — there is little room for more, so evaporation is slow. This is why washing dries more slowly on a humid, cloudy day than on a dry day inland.

[*] Remember! Evaporation is FASTER when it is hot, when the surface is large, when there is wind, and when the air is dry. Evaporation is SLOWER when it is cool, when the surface is small, when the air is still, and when the air is humid.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Sweating cools your body using evaporation. When sweat evaporates from your skin, it carries heat away, which is why a breeze feels so refreshing on a hot day in Kismaayo. For thousands of years people along coasts have made salt by letting the sun evaporate seawater in shallow pools — one of the oldest uses of science in human history.

concepts.title: The Water Cycle - Water on a Never-Ending Journey
concepts.explanation:
Now let us put evaporation and condensation together to understand one of the grandest systems on Earth: the water cycle. This is the endless journey that water takes as it moves between the ocean, the sky, and the land. It is powered by energy from the sun, and it brings the rains that fill our rivers and grow our crops. Let us follow a single drop of water on its journey.

Evaporation. The sun shines on the Indian Ocean and warms the surface. Water evaporates, rising into the sky as invisible water vapour. Water also evaporates from lakes, rivers, and even from the leaves of acacia and mango trees, which release water vapour in a process called transpiration.

Condensation and clouds. High in the sky the air is much cooler. As the water vapour rises and cools, it condenses into countless tiny water droplets. Billions of these droplets together form the clouds you see drifting over Mogadishu and Hargeisa.

Precipitation. When the droplets in a cloud join together and grow heavy enough, they fall back to Earth as rain. In our region the great rains of the Gu season arrive this way, turning the dry land green. In colder parts of the world, precipitation can fall as snow.

Collection and runoff. The rain that falls collects in seasonal rivers, in wells, and in the ground. Some flows across the land, filling the Jubba River, and eventually makes its way back to the Indian Ocean. And then the sun warms the sea once more, and the whole journey begins again.

This cycle never stops and never runs out. The water that brings the Gu rains has travelled this path countless times before. Understanding it helps us see why we must protect our water: the same water is shared by everyone and must be used wisely. Keeping wells clean, not wasting water, and caring for the land are all ways of being a good khalifah, a caretaker of the earth that we have been trusted with.
concepts.example: Did You Know? In our region there are two main rainy seasons: the Gu rains around April to June, and the shorter Deyr rains later in the year. Both are brought by the water cycle. Not a single new drop of water has been added to Earth in millions of years. The water cycle simply recycles the water we already have, over and over.

concepts.title: Dissolving - When a Solid Seems to Disappear
concepts.explanation:
There is one more everyday change to understand: dissolving. When you stir a spoonful of sugar into a cup of hot shaah, the sugar seems to vanish. Where does it go? The sugar has dissolved. It has not disappeared and it has not melted — the tiny sugar particles have spread out and slipped into the spaces between the water particles, mixing so completely that you can no longer see them. You know the sugar is still there because the tea tastes sweet. A mixture like this, where a solid is completely dissolved in a liquid, is called a solution.

The same thing happens when salt dissolves in water. And here is a lovely connection: if you leave that salty water in the sun, the water will evaporate away and leave the salt behind, visible once more. This is precisely how salt is collected from seawater along the coast. Dissolving hides the solid; evaporation brings it back. Two ideas from this unit working together.

Some things dissolve and some do not. Sugar and salt dissolve well in water. Sand and small stones do not dissolve — stir them as much as you like and they still settle at the bottom. Warm water usually dissolves things faster than cold water, because the faster-moving particles mix more quickly. That is why sugar dissolves more easily in hot tea than in cold.
concepts.example: It is important to remember that dissolving is not the same as melting, even though both can make a solid seem to change. Melting happens when heat alone turns a solid into a liquid, like ice becoming water, and it needs no second substance. Dissolving needs a liquid to mix into, like the water in your tea, and it can happen without any extra heat at all. Keeping these two ideas separate is one of the marks of a careful scientist, so pause and check yourself whenever you use these words.

methods.title: Sorting the States of Matter
methods.example: To observe and sort household materials into solids, liquids, and gases by testing their properties. Make a Prediction: Before you start, write down: How will you tell a solid from a liquid? What test could show that air (a gas) is really there?
steps: Take each solid and place it in different cups. Does it change shape? Does it keep its size? Record your answer.
Pour a little water into a tall cup, then into a wide bowl. Does the shape change? Does the amount change? Record it.
Do the same test with the cooking oil and the milk.
Blow air into the balloon or trap air in the bag. Squeeze it gently. Can you feel the gas pushing back? Does it fill the whole balloon?
Fill in your results table below.

methods.title: Watching Ice Melt (A State Change)
methods.example: To observe melting — a solid changing to a liquid — and see how a warmer place speeds it up. Make a Prediction Which ice cube will melt faster: one left in a warm sunny spot, or one left in a cool shady spot? Write your guess and why.
steps: Place one ice cube on each plate.
Put one plate in a warm, sunny place and the other in a cool, shady place.
Start your timer. Every 5 minutes, look at both cubes and write down how much has melted.
Record the time when each cube has completely melted.

methods.title: The Great Evaporation Race
methods.example: To carry out a fair test showing how surface area affects how fast water evaporates. Make a Prediction: Two equal amounts of water: one in a wide shallow dish, one in a narrow tall cup. Which will dry up first? Write your prediction and your reason.
steps: Pour exactly the same amount of water into the wide dish and the tall cup.
Mark the starting water level on each container.
Place both in the same warm, sunny place, side by side, so temperature and wind are the same for both. The ONLY thing different is the surface area.
Check twice a day and mark the new water level with the time.
Continue until one container is empty. Record which dried up first.

methods.title: Catching Condensation
methods.example: To make condensation happen and understand that water vapour in the air can turn back into liquid. Make a Prediction: What will appear on the outside of a cold glass left in the room? Where do you think that water comes from?
steps: Wipe the outside of the cup completely dry so you know it starts dry.
Fill the cup with cold water and add ice if you have it.
Place it on a table and wait 5 to 10 minutes without touching it.
Look closely at the outside of the cup. Gently touch it. What do you feel and see? Record it.

methods.title: A Mini Water Cycle in a Bowl
methods.example: To build a small model of the water cycle and watch evaporation, condensation, and 'rain' happen. Make a Prediction: If warm water sits in a covered bowl in the sun, what will happen to the water? Where will droplets appear?
steps: Pour a little warm water into the bottom of the large bowl (this is your 'ocean'). Do not fill it.
Stand the empty small cup in the middle of the bowl, keeping it dry inside (this is your 'land').
Cover the whole bowl tightly with cling film so no air escapes.
Place the small stone on the cling film right above the empty cup, so the film dips down slightly toward the cup.
Put the bowl in a warm, sunny spot and watch for 30 to 60 minutes.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 1
workedExamples.prompt: Which state of matter keeps both a definite shape and a definite volume? (a) solid (b) liquid (c) gas (d) none of them
workedExamples.solution: 1. (a) solid. Only solids keep both a fixed shape and a fixed volume because their particles are locked in place.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: In which state are the particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions? (a) solid (b) liquid (c) gas (d) ice
workedExamples.solution: 2. (c) gas. Gas particles are spread far apart and move quickly in every direction.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: A liquid poured from a cup into a bowl will: (a) change its amount (b) keep its shape (c) take the shape of the bowl (d) turn into a gas
workedExamples.solution: 3. (c) take the shape of the bowl. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the container's shape; the amount does not change.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Melting is the change from: (a) liquid to solid (b) solid to liquid (c) liquid to gas (d) gas to liquid
workedExamples.solution: 4. (b) solid to liquid. Melting is a solid becoming a liquid when heated.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which change needs heat to be REMOVED? (a) melting (b) evaporation (c) boiling (d) freezing
workedExamples.solution: 5. (d) freezing. Freezing needs heat removed so particles slow and lock into a solid. The others all need heat added.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Evaporation happens: (a) only at boiling point (b) at any temperature, at the surface (c) only in a freezer (d) only at night
workedExamples.solution: 6. (b) at any temperature, at the surface. Only surface particles with enough energy escape; boiling is not required.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which factor does NOT speed up evaporation? (a) more heat (b) more wind (c) a smaller surface area (d) drier air
workedExamples.solution: 7. (c) a smaller surface area. A smaller surface slows evaporation; the other three all speed it up.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: Water droplets forming on a cold glass is an example of: (a) melting (b) condensation (c) freezing (d) dissolving
workedExamples.solution: 8. (b) condensation. Water vapour in the air cools on the glass and turns to liquid.

practice.answer: 1. (a) solid. Only solids keep both a fixed shape and a fixed volume because their particles are locked in place.

activities.title: Sorting the States of Matter
activities.materials: A few solids: a stone, a wooden spoon, a metal key, a dried date.; A few liquids: water, cooking oil, camel milk or any milk.; A gas: a balloon or a plastic bag you can trap air in.; Two or three cups or bowls of different shapes.
steps: Take each solid and place it in different cups. Does it change shape? Does it keep its size? Record your answer.
Pour a little water into a tall cup, then into a wide bowl. Does the shape change? Does the amount change? Record it.
Do the same test with the cooking oil and the milk.
Blow air into the balloon or trap air in the bag. Squeeze it gently. Can you feel the gas pushing back? Does it fill the whole balloon?
Fill in your results table below.
Safety: Plastic bags are not toys — never put them over or near your face.

activities.title: Watching Ice Melt (A State Change)
activities.materials: Two ice cubes of the same size (freeze water in a freezer if you have one).; Two small plates or saucers.; A clock or a phone timer.; A warm sunny spot and a cool shady spot.
steps: Place one ice cube on each plate.
Put one plate in a warm, sunny place and the other in a cool, shady place.
Start your timer. Every 5 minutes, look at both cubes and write down how much has melted.
Record the time when each cube has completely melted.

activities.title: The Great Evaporation Race
activities.materials: A wide shallow dish or plate.; A narrow tall cup or glass.; The same amount of water for each (measure with the same cup).; A marker or tape to mark the water level, and a sunny windowsill.
steps: Pour exactly the same amount of water into the wide dish and the tall cup.
Mark the starting water level on each container.
Place both in the same warm, sunny place, side by side, so temperature and wind are the same for both. The ONLY thing different is the surface area.
Check twice a day and mark the new water level with the time.
Continue until one container is empty. Record which dried up first.

activities.title: Catching Condensation
activities.materials: A clean glass or metal cup.; Cold water and, if you have them, a few ice cubes.; A dry cloth to wipe the outside of the cup first.
steps: Wipe the outside of the cup completely dry so you know it starts dry.
Fill the cup with cold water and add ice if you have it.
Place it on a table and wait 5 to 10 minutes without touching it.
Look closely at the outside of the cup. Gently touch it. What do you feel and see? Record it.

activities.title: A Mini Water Cycle in a Bowl
activities.materials: A large bowl.; A small empty cup that fits inside the bowl.; Warm (not boiling) water — ask an adult to help.; Cling film or a clear plastic bag to cover the bowl.; A small stone or pebble.
steps: Pour a little warm water into the bottom of the large bowl (this is your 'ocean'). Do not fill it.
Stand the empty small cup in the middle of the bowl, keeping it dry inside (this is your 'land').
Cover the whole bowl tightly with cling film so no air escapes.
Place the small stone on the cling film right above the empty cup, so the film dips down slightly toward the cup.
Put the bowl in a warm, sunny spot and watch for 30 to 60 minutes.
Safety: Plastic bags are not toys — never put them over or near your face. Hot water must be poured and carried by an adult only.

activities.title: Observe: Dissolving - When a Solid Seems to Disappear
activities.materials: A few solids: a stone, a wooden spoon, a metal key, a dried date.; A few liquids: water, cooking oil, camel milk or any milk.; A gas: a balloon or a plastic bag you can trap air in.; Two or three cups or bowls of different shapes.
steps: Look for an example of dissolving — when a solid seems to disappear around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Temperature and Surface area.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: The Three States of Matter
rules.text: Let us begin with what you can see and touch.

rules.title: The Particle Model — The Secret Inside Matter
rules.text: Now we come to one of the biggest ideas in all of science.

rules.title: Changing State — The Power of Heating and Cooling
rules.text: How does one state turn into another?

rules.title: Evaporation and the Factors That Affect It
rules.text: Evaporation deserves special attention because it happens all around you, all the time, and understanding it is genuinely useful.

rules.title: The Water Cycle — Water on a Never-Ending Journey
rules.text: Now let us put evaporation and condensation together to understand one of the grandest systems on Earth: the water cycle.

rules.title: Dissolving — When a Solid Seems to Disappear
rules.text: There is one more everyday change to understand: dissolving.

terms: The tiny pieces, too small to see, that all matter is made of.
Solid to liquid, when heat is added (ice at 0 degrees Celsius).
Liquid to solid, when heat is removed (water at 0 degrees Celsius).
Liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature.
Fast liquid to gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point (water at 100 degrees Celsius).
Gas to liquid, when it cools.
Water in its invisible gas form.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail.

vocabulary.example: At a certain temperature, called the melting point, they gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and begin sliding around each other.
The shallow pan spreads the water out over a much larger surface area than the deep bucket.

Humidity is the amount of water vapour already in the air.

Melting and dissolving are mixed up.
You cannot see them, so they seem like nothing.

realProblems.prompt: Halima wants the washing to dry as fast as possible. Give her three pieces of advice based on the factors affecting evaporation, and explain each one.
realProblems.answer: 1. (i) Hang the washing in the hot sun — heat gives particles energy to escape. (ii) Spread the clothes out wide — a larger surface area lets more water escape. (iii) Hang them where the wind blows — moving air carries damp air away so more water can evaporate. (Drier air / low humidity also helps.)

(Drier air / low humidity also helps.)

realProblems.answer: 2. The water changes from liquid to gas (boiling/evaporation), and steam rises. Boiling heats the water to 100 degrees Celsius, which kills harmful germs in it, making the water safe to drink once it cools.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe how the particles are arranged in a solid.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1. In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a fixed, regular pattern and only vibrate on the spot. This is why solids keep their shape.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a liquid can be poured but a solid cannot.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2. In a liquid the particles can slide past one another, so a liquid flows and can be poured. In a solid the particles are locked in place, so it cannot flow.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What happens to the particles of ice when it is heated until it melts?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3. When ice is heated, its particles vibrate faster until they gain enough energy to break free and slide around each other. The solid ice becomes liquid water.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the four factors that affect how fast a liquid evaporates.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4. Temperature, surface area, air movement (wind), and humidity.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why do wet clothes dry faster on a hot, windy day than on a cool, still day?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5. Heat gives the water particles more energy to escape, and wind carries the damp air away so more particles can leave. Both factors speed up evaporation.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. Evaporation is slow, happens only at the surface, and can occur at any temperature. Boiling is fast, happens throughout the liquid with bubbles, and occurs at the boiling point (100 degrees Celsius for water).

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a gas?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the air in a balloon. Air is a gas; the others are solids or a liquid.

games.title: Challenge Cards: Melting
games.description: Practise melting through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Evaporation happens:
choices: at any temperature, at the surface
rounds.answer: at any temperature, at the surface
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: at any temperature, at the surface. Only surface particles with enough energy escape; boiling is not required.

rounds.prompt: In the water cycle, the sun's energy mainly causes:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: evaporation. The sun's heat drives water up from the sea and land as vapour.

rounds.prompt: Boiling is different from evaporation because boiling:
choices: is fast with bubbles all through the liquid
rounds.answer: is fast with bubbles all through the liquid
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: fast with bubbles all through the liquid. Boiling is rapid and happens throughout; evaporation is slow and only at the surface.

rounds.prompt: A liquid poured from a cup into a bowl will:
choices: take the shape of the bowl
rounds.answer: take the shape of the bowl
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: take the shape of the bowl. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the container's shape; the amount does not change.

rounds.prompt: Which factor does NOT speed up evaporation?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.

rounds.prompt: When sugar is stirred into tea and seems to vanish, it has:

rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: solid. Only solids keep both a fixed shape and a fixed volume because their particles are locked in place.

selfAssessment: I can name and describe the three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas, and give examples of each from your own home.
I can explain the particle model — that all matter is made of tiny particles, and describe how those particles are arranged and how they move in each state.
I can describe state changes — melting, freezing, evaporation, condensing, and boiling — and explain how heating and cooling cause them.
I can explain evaporation and identify the four main factors that make a liquid evaporate faster: temperature, surface area, air movement, and humidity.
I can describe the water cycle and explain how evaporation and condensation move water between the ocean, the sky, and the land.
I can plan a fair test to investigate what affects evaporation, and record your results carefully.
I can use scientific words correctly when you write and talk about matter.
I can name two other factors mentioned in the passage that help the fish dry faster.
